name: Design System Audit
definition: A design system audit is a structured review of a system's assets, implementation, guidance, and use in products. It identifies gaps and inconsistencies so teams can decide what to fix, consolidate, document, or retire.
contentMarkdown:
# Design System Audit

A design system audit is a structured review of a system's assets, implementation, guidance, and use in products. It identifies gaps and inconsistencies so teams can decide what to fix, consolidate, document, or retire.

## What should a design system audit cover?

Set the scope before gathering findings. Record the products, libraries, packages, versions, flows, and dates included.

| Area | Questions to investigate |
|---|---|
| Design assets | Are components current, findable, and clearly named? |
| Code | Which implementations and versions are actually used? |
| Tokens | Are roles consistent, and where are values overridden? |
| Documentation | Do examples match supported APIs and behavior? |
| Product experience | Do shared parts work together in real tasks? |
| Ownership | Can teams resolve a gap or request a change? |

A visual inventory is a useful starting point. It cannot establish whether the code API, keyboard behavior, or maintenance process is correct.

## Example: three implementations of a date field

Suppose an audit finds three date fields with similar appearance. One uses the current shared component, one uses an old version, and one is a local implementation.

Check why each exists. The local field may support a genuine requirement the shared component lacks. The old version may be blocked by a compatibility issue.

Record the evidence, affected tasks, likely impact, owner, and proposed next step. “Replace everything with the newest field” is premature until the team understands those differences.

## How do you turn findings into action?

Group findings by cause, such as an unclear API, a missing interaction state, or an outdated migration guide. Separate a correction to one product from a change to the shared system.

Prioritize by user impact, repetition, dependencies, and effort. Assign a concrete outcome: fix a focus problem, document an exception, consolidate a duplicate, or retire an unsupported asset.

Keep a record of what was inspected. An audit covering two flows should not be reported as a complete organization-wide assessment.

## Design system audit vs. accessibility audit

An audit can find accessibility problems, but a design system inventory is not a WCAG conformance evaluation. That requires a defined accessibility scope and appropriate evaluation methods.

Likewise, passing component checks does not establish accessibility for every consuming page. Use a [web accessibility audit](/glossary/web-accessibility-audit.html) and task testing where the question concerns complete experiences.

Repeat the relevant checks after remediation. A backlog entry marked complete is not evidence that the original discrepancy has disappeared.

## Related terms

- [Design System Adoption](/glossary/design-system-adoption.html)
- [Design System Metrics](/glossary/design-system-metrics.html)
- [Design Debt](/glossary/design-debt.html)
- [Web Accessibility Audit](/glossary/web-accessibility-audit.html)

## Sources

- [Contribution criteria, GOV.UK Design System](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/community/contribution-criteria/)
- [USWDS maturity model](https://designsystem.digital.gov/maturity-model/)
- [Evaluating Web Accessibility, W3C WAI](https://www.w3.org/WAI/test-evaluate/)

name: Design System Documentation
definition: Design system documentation explains how to use, implement, and maintain a design system. It connects reusable components and tokens to the decisions teams need to make when building a product.
contentMarkdown:
# Design System Documentation

Design system documentation explains how to use, implement, and maintain a design system. It connects reusable components and tokens to the decisions teams need to make when building a product.

## What should design system documentation include?

Organize guidance around questions people need to answer while working.

| Question | Useful documentation |
|---|---|
| Should I use this component? | Purpose, suitable scenarios, and alternatives |
| How does it behave? | States, keyboard interaction, validation, and responsive behavior |
| How do I implement it? | Supported API, imports, token references, and working examples |
| What can change? | Ownership, release status, compatibility, and migration guidance |

A screenshot shows appearance. A working example can expose behavior. Written guidance explains the conditions and decisions that neither makes obvious.

## Example: documenting an address field

Suppose a shared address field supports autocomplete and manual entry. Document what happens when no suggestion matches, whether users can edit the returned address, and how validation errors appear.

Provide an example with a long address, an unavailable lookup service, and a keyboard-only interaction. Specify which component version the example uses. The application still owns delivery rules and whether an address is accepted.

This gives a product team enough information to choose and integrate the field without copying a screenshot and inventing the missing behavior.

## Documentation vs. a component catalog

A [component library](/glossary/component-libraries.html) provides reusable implementations. Its catalog shows the available parts. Documentation also explains when those parts are appropriate and how to combine them into a task.

[Storybook](/glossary/storybook.html) can present rendered component states and implementation details. Broader guidance may live beside it or elsewhere, provided the links and ownership stay clear. A generated list of properties does not explain the product decisions behind those properties.

## How do you keep documentation useful?

Start with a frequent task and its most consequential mistakes. Link the guidance from the places where people select or implement the component. Ask a teammate to complete the task using only that guidance, and record where they need help.

Update examples when the component changes. Assign an owner who can correct discrepancies between the guidance, design assets, and released code. Archive superseded instructions with a visible route to the current version.

For AI-assisted implementation, expose the same supported APIs and examples in a form the agent can retrieve. Verify its output against the implementation: machine-readable documentation can still be incomplete or outdated.

## Related terms

- [Design System](/glossary/design-system.html)
- [Component Architecture](/glossary/component-architecture.html)
- [Storybook](/glossary/storybook.html)
- [Design System Governance](/glossary/design-system-governance.html)

## Sources

- [Button guidance, GOV.UK Design System](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/button/)
- [Autodocs, Storybook](https://storybook.js.org/docs/writing-docs/autodocs)

name: Design System Metrics
definition: Design system metrics are measures used to understand a design system's use, quality, operating effort, and effects on product work. A useful metric answers a specific decision rather than simply reporting how many components exist.
sources: Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale, Google Research (https://research.google/pubs/measuring-the-user-experience-on-a-large-scale-user-centered-metrics-for-web-applications/)
contentMarkdown:
# Design System Metrics

Design system metrics are measures used to understand a design system's use, quality, operating effort, and effects on product work. A useful metric answers a specific decision rather than simply reporting how many components exist.

## Which design system metrics are useful?

Start with a goal, identify observable signals, and define a measure. Google's HEART research describes this goals-to-metrics approach for user experience; the following design system examples are practical applications, not a required HEART scorecard.

| Decision | Possible measure | Important boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Where is adoption blocked? | Eligible products using supported components | Define eligibility and version |
| Are releases difficult to consume? | Time to complete a specified migration | Compare similar changes and team conditions |
| Is quality improving? | Verified recurring defects in sampled flows | Keep inspection scope consistent |
| Is support sustainable? | Resolution time and repeated support requests | Fewer requests can also mean disengagement |

Use a small set that informs an actual decision. A single overall “system health” score can hide why a result changed.

## Example: measuring field reuse

Suppose an audit finds that 36 of 60 eligible field instances use the shared component. Coverage in that sample is 60%.

After a migration, repeat the same inspection rules. Report changes in the sample and eligibility rules alongside the result. A package download count cannot substitute for this instance-level measure.

If teams also report faster implementation, define the task and include review and rework time. Comparing an initial complex field with a later simple field would not isolate the system's contribution.

## Metrics vs. component telemetry

[Component telemetry](/glossary/component-telemetry.html) is one way to collect usage or behavior data. Metrics define what those observations mean for a decision.

A metric may instead come from a code inventory, a support log, a task study, or a documented survey. Choose the method that fits the question and the privacy constraints.

## How do you estimate design system ROI?

ROI compares estimated benefits with costs over a stated period. One conventional expression is `(benefit − cost) ÷ cost`.

Include maintenance, documentation, support, migration, and consumer effort in the relevant cost scope. State how saved time was estimated and whether it actually became available for other work. Avoid converting every reused component into a fixed number of saved hours.

Report measured outcomes separately from modeled financial benefits. If attribution is uncertain, present assumptions and a range instead of a precise-looking promise.

## Related terms

- [Design System Adoption](/glossary/design-system-adoption.html)
- [Component Telemetry](/glossary/component-telemetry.html)
- [Design System Audit](/glossary/design-system-audit.html)
- [DesignOps](/glossary/designops.html)

## Sources

- [Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale, Google Research](https://research.google/pubs/measuring-the-user-experience-on-a-large-scale-user-centered-metrics-for-web-applications/)
- [Design Systems Report 2026, Zeroheight](https://report.zeroheight.com/2026)

name: Design System Migration
definition: A design system migration moves products from one set of shared design resources or implementations to another. It can involve component versions, token names, design libraries, APIs, documentation, and the workflows that depend on them.
sources: Migration guide overview, Carbon Design System (https://www.carbondesignsystem.com/getting-started/migrating/guide/overview)
contentMarkdown:
# Design System Migration

A design system migration moves products from one set of shared design resources or implementations to another. It can involve component versions, token names, design libraries, APIs, documentation, and the workflows that depend on them.

## Migration vs. versioning

[Versioning](/glossary/design-system-versioning-semver.html) communicates changes under a defined compatibility policy. Migration is the work consuming teams perform to adopt them.

A change described as a visual refresh may still alter layout, interaction, or API expectations. Identify the actual consumer impact rather than assuming the release label describes all necessary work.

## A practical migration plan

| Step | What to establish |
|---|---|
| Inventory | Affected products, versions, overrides, and owners |
| Map changes | Replacements, removed options, and intentional behavior differences |
| Pilot | One representative flow with meaningful edge cases |
| Validate | Behavior, accessibility, visual changes, and integration |
| Roll out | Team responsibilities, sequence, support, and retirement conditions |

Record the starting state so the team can distinguish migration effects from other product changes.

## Example: replacing a date picker

Suppose a new shared date picker changes its value format and error behavior. Updating the import alone would leave the consuming form with the wrong assumptions.

The pilot checks parsing, locale display, keyboard operation, invalid dates, and the submitted value. It also reviews layout with existing error messages and help text.

The team documents the mapping, updates design examples, and identifies which remaining flows need manual attention. A codemod may help with a mechanical replacement; it cannot decide every interaction or business rule.

## How do you manage a phased migration?

Define what can coexist, for how long, and who maintains compatibility during the transition. Make exceptions and blockers visible.

Give consumers a tested example and a way to request support. Publish deprecation and removal conditions with enough practical information to act on them. Carbon's migration documentation is an example of separating design and development guidance for a specific system change.

Plan recovery for a failed rollout. Reverting a UI package does not necessarily reverse related data or configuration changes.

## When is the migration complete?

Use explicit acceptance criteria, such as verified target versions, resolved exceptions, updated documentation, and the removal of unsupported resources.

Check representative product tasks after rollout. A completed dependency update is evidence of a code change, not by itself evidence that the migrated experience works.

## Related terms

- [Design System Versioning and SemVer](/glossary/design-system-versioning-semver.html)
- [Design System Adoption](/glossary/design-system-adoption.html)
- [Design System Audit](/glossary/design-system-audit.html)
- [Design QA](/glossary/design-qa.html)

## Sources

- [Migration guide overview, Carbon Design System](https://www.carbondesignsystem.com/getting-started/migrating/guide/overview)
- [Semantic Versioning 2.0.0](https://semver.org/)

name: Theming
definition: Theming is the practice of applying a coordinated set of design values to a shared interface. In a design system, a theme can change colors, typography, or other supported decisions while components retain a consistent purpose and API.
contentMarkdown:
# Theming

Theming is the practice of applying a coordinated set of design values to a shared interface. In a design system, a theme can change colors, typography, or other supported decisions while components retain a consistent purpose and API.

## How does theming work with design tokens?

A component can request a semantic role such as `color.text.primary`. A theme supplies the value for that role. The component does not need a separate implementation for each palette.

Illustrative mappings might look like this:

| Role | Light theme | Dark theme |
|---|---|---|
| Primary text | A dark neutral | A light neutral |
| Page surface | A light neutral | A dark neutral |
| Link text | A darker brand color | A lighter brand color |

The table describes roles, not tested color combinations. Verify the actual values and states in the product.

## Theme vs. mode vs. component variant

A **theme** groups coordinated values. A design tool's **mode** is one mechanism for selecting values in a variable collection. A **component variant** represents a supported variation, such as primary and secondary button emphasis.

These concepts can work together, but changing a Figma mode does not by itself implement the corresponding runtime theme. Design assets, generated tokens, and application styles need an agreed mapping.

## Example: two brands with light and dark appearances

Suppose two booking products share a component library. Both use the same field behavior and keyboard interactions, but each has its own accent and typography choices. Each brand also supports light and dark appearances.

Keep brand identity and color appearance explicit. Decide which combinations are supported, how a user preference is selected and retained, and what happens when no preference is available.

A component may use a component-specific token that points to a semantic role. Keep that indirection only when it gives the team a useful scope for future changes.

## What should you test across themes?

Check readable text, focus indicators, control boundaries, validation states, selected states, and charts. Review images and icons that may disappear or convey the wrong meaning on a different surface.

Test in the application, including nested surfaces and overlays. A token palette cannot establish accessibility for every foreground and background pairing.

For multi-brand systems, document which differences are intentional and which behavior stays shared. A theme should not silently change what an action does.

## Related terms

- [Semantic Tokens](/glossary/semantic-tokens.html)
- [Figma Variables and Modes](/glossary/figma-variables-modes.html)
- [Design Tokens](/glossary/design-tokens.html)
- [WCAG Color Contrast](/glossary/wcag-color-contrast.html)

## Sources

- [Design tokens and theming, Atlassian](https://developer.atlassian.com/platform/forge/design-tokens-and-theming/)
- [Contrast (Minimum), W3C WAI](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html)
